edges.description: IKK-alpha is required for embryonic keratinocytes to complete terminal differentiation. Shown in mice; the human report states the same role for CHUK.
Undifferentiated epidermis cannot form a normal skin, leaving the thin, membrane-like covering that binds the limbs.

Differentiating epidermis signals to underlying mesoderm. When differentiation fails, that signalling is disturbed. The rescue experiment locates the defect in the epidermis; that it acts through disturbed epidermal-mesodermal interaction is the authors' interpretation.
The abnormal skin is itself the transparent covering.
The abnormal limb skin lacks its adnexal structures.

nodes.description: The initiating lesion. A homozygous CHUK point mutation in the affected fetuses led to loss of IKK-alpha, a subunit of the IkappaB kinase complex. Because the protein is absent, its kinase activity is lost and is bound below; the downstream epidermal effect, however, depends on a kinase-independent activity of IKK-alpha (PMID:15071597), so the kinase term records what is lost, not the route to the phenotype.

nodes.description: Targeted disruption of the gene encoding IKK-alpha. Knockout mice die perinatally, with severely impaired limb outgrowth and hyperproliferative, poorly differentiated epidermis. Two independent knockout lines were reported in 1999 (PMID:10195895, PMID:10195896).

evidence.reference_title: Limb and skin abnormalities in mice lacking IKKalpha.
evidence.snippet: IKKalpha-deficient mice died perinatally. In IKKalpha-deficient fetuses, limb outgrowth was severely impaired despite unaffected skeletal development.

nodes.description: IKK-alpha-deficient mice in which IKK-alpha is restored only in basal epidermal keratinocytes. Epidermal differentiation and skeletal morphology are normal, which places the skeletal defect downstream of the epidermis.

evidence.reference_title: IkappaB kinase-alpha acts in the epidermis to control skeletal and craniofacial morphogenesis.
evidence.snippet: We tested this hypothesis by introducing an epidermal-specific Ikka (also known as Chuk) transgene into IKK-alpha-deficient mice.

nodes.description: In IKK-alpha-deficient mice, failed epidermal differentiation is proposed to disturb the signalling between epidermis and mesoderm that shapes the skeleton. One identified component is loss of repression of FGF family members such as FGF8, whose expression is raised in limb-bud ectoderm.

evidence.reference_title: IkappaB kinase-alpha acts in the epidermis to control skeletal and craniofacial morphogenesis.
evidence.snippet: One way by which IKK-alpha controls skeletal and craniofacial morphogenesis is by repressing expression of fibroblast growth factor (FGF) family members, such as FGF8, whose expression is specifically elevated in the limb bud ectoderm of IKK-alpha-deficient mice.

nodes.description: Without IKK-alpha, embryonic epidermal keratinocytes keep proliferating and do not complete terminal differentiation. The requirement is met by a kinase-independent activity of IKK-alpha, and mice lacking IKK-alpha still activate the IKK complex and degrade IkappaB in response to inflammatory stimuli, so the defect is not a general failure of cytokine-induced NF-kappaB activation.
